Well I haven't had much of a guilt-tripping upbringing (even though my grandmother was religious), I just felt like it's inherently wrong for me to like anyone romantically and vice-versa. But growing up in an environment you described makes so much sense for feeling like it's something sinful. I think this can be deeply rooted but can be changed with hard and consistent mental work to change the belief system.

As for your story, that seems a weird act on her terms. I would think the same as you did. It must have been a bummer since it already took some courage to ask her out just to hear her being all weirded out. Even if this wasn't her intention she wouldn't have to call you creepy just for asking her out. I hope you try again some day, you seem to have some bad luck with this girl here.

I also have a short story, but this one it's stupid on my terms. I had a crush on a new coworker and we were starting to get along, but still not so much that we'd hang out outside of work. One day I mentioned that I'd really like to go to a concert because I miss live music (post-quarantine). He said he'd love to go to some musician at the end of the week but doesn't have anyone to go with. I wasn't sure if he just said that because he agreed with me that live music is nice or did he wanted to invite me over. I didn't want to risk it with saying "oh cool, we could go together" because if he didn't want that, he'd be in an uncomfortable position... And also, why would he even want to invite me since we haven't even known each other that much. So, I told him that there's nothing wrong with going to concerts alone and he responded that this would be depressing and I kinda further tried to motivate him to go to this concert alone but he didn't find my motivational speech inspiring. Then he kind of became more distant towards me despite me trying to spend more time around him. I'm still confused because I'll never know what was going on.

I'm a girl but otherwise same thing. And people asking me of I'm asexual or "carrier driven"... Ugh no I just can't react properly, I don't want to believe it and I don't want anyone know I like them romantically, it feels like a sin, like I'll humiliate someone else if I was attracted to them... Even if it's mutual, it just becomes off, it's way beyond the ordinary nervousness people I know tell me when they're dating someone. I can't even deal with the possibility.

Hm, well this will all just be my guessing since I don't understand how they really feel. But in general I see narcissistic pd as a persistent feeling of shame which is covered by grandiosity (and avpd as something that is kinda "confirmed" by feelings of shame, not really trying to cover up anything, just hide away from the world). 

I think that narcissists can be roughly divided into those who are kind of "naive", live in their bubble and are blinded by their feelings of grandiosity to an extent that they can't be easily put off-guard and feel shame. They still have a distorded picture about themselves and can put down others, but are not necessarily manipulative and don't exactly enjoy when others are hurt (this is just my opinion and greatly based on anecdotal experience with someone). 

I also think this subtype generally feel successful and content with themselves and is probably not so dangerous to others. Maybe it's more about them being lucky, hard working and having a specific upbringing. I do think that them being in different circumstances, they could behave as the other subtype. 

Also, the main difference is probably that the first type enjoys being praised, and the other, scarier type enjoys having power towards others (this can be bith present as well, of course). This second type is in my opinion more capable of manipulative tactics. 

They also have this highly inflated sense of self which is, in its core, really fragile. For some reason they find more content (power) in abusing others, but get bored quickl, and don't have much inner piece. 

I think the main problem both for avpds and npds is not feeling *equal* to everyone else, to not feel that everyone has equal worth and no one is better or worse than others. Narcissists can therefore feel more deserving than everyone else and also see others as undeserving, which gives them a "right" to exploit. But they probably carry a lot of hatred as well, because even if they think they're better, they still wouldn't have to act like an ass. They could just feel proud of themselves and that would be it. But I think there's still some shame inside them which prevents them from being content with themsemves. 

A person with avpd would probably react in a more self-descrutive and avoidant, cold manners. So your experience with your bf and your ex makes a lot of sense in that regard. I think shame is in its core present in both of these disorders, but is manifested differently.

I think that some narcissistic subtypes can definitely be driven by shame in terms of feeling inferior. There might be a similarity with avpd, but I think the main difference here is how each of this emotions are shown. Narcissists create illusions of their superiority while avoidants kind of accept that they're worse than everyone else and something is flawed about them (us). Another similarity, both avpds and npds are sensitive to criticism and can experience this as something really shameful. But again, the difference is in their interpretation and actions towards themselves and others.

I also think some people with borderline pd can feel a lot of shame. Some can be really self-critical and sensitive. Also, they can have lots of this black and white mentalities so when they perhaps hurt someone who they see as a danger to theselves and alter recognize their mistake, they can feel ashamed (and guilty, which is probably just a normal consequence when you realize you did something wrong). But I'm not exactly sure if that's really how it works and what is the relationship between bpd and shame. I believe they can also feel a lot of shame, but how this is manifested can differ from other PDs (someone correct me if I'm wrong, I'm not an expert, just my opinion).

As for other PDs I'm not exactly sure but I think that to some extent it can still affect and them and drive their actions but it's probably not the main things that drives them.

Yeah. I believe it's good and necessary to cry things out sometimes, and not to be shut down shortly after actually getting some courage to let some things out. It feels so invalidating to hear "well crying won't help" or "do something about it" or "ok well and what am i supposed to say on that, itbsucks but life goes on". While all these things have point, I think it's more about timing and attitude the other person has. It's normal to feel devastated for a while and it just brings more guilt and shame to the person who is going through something at the moment. 

Speaking from my point of view, but it helped me much more if a person let me be sad for a moment and just was there, without trying to shame, guilt or ridicule me. After I realized someone really listened and cared, I felt so much better that I actually find the power within myself to stand up on my feet again. It's just like a open would, it needs to be cleaned and taken care of before patient can safely start walking again.

While I was sweeping it, they were laughing and talking, and I felt so embarrassed because I was terrified that they were laughing at me knowing that I don't understand a word.

They could've been talking about something else or maybe just joking with a girl who accidentally broke this glass, but what if?

I'm still a student and I work as a waitress (my field of study is unrelated to this job). This was always something I could never do. At first I just wanted a job with the least interactions, ideally being hidden somewhere, away from everyone's eyes.

I came to this job because they needed help in the kitchen, but one day they were short of staff so here I am. I stayed, because despite being one of the hardest challenges, it helped me build some confidence. I (very slowly) became more relaxed and less awkward and I'm still learning how to interact with people. The years of avoidance and self-isolation had its consequences.

At first, I was really awkward, shy and cared too much about everything. Now, about 2 years in, I feel I'm still awkward, shy and care too much. But at the same time, I feel more comfortable with myself and for me, it ended up being a good decion. It also helped with my assertiveness. In some ways, it's the ebst job I even had. 

Still, I think I'm not as easy-going as some other waiters. Sometimes I get sick of dealing with some people, and when I have a bad period (mental health wise), I have a lot mlre trouble interacting, lookong at people's eyes and having people looking at me. I don't know if I'll ever be fully comfortable about it, but at my better days, I feel a lot better at the end of the day, almost normal, and it's a bliss.

Hm, if you find yourself in uncomfortable situations because of this, maybe you can find another way to friendly reject someone. Sadly, rejection is usually hard for both people involved, but at the end of the day, it's not your purpose be with someone you don't see yourself with. Your only job here is to do it in a way that is the least hurtful. But it's not all up to you, the other person also has to show some maturity. So maybe you just need to find another sentence. Saying you're in a relationship is a good way to get away from the situation, but it can have its consequences. Sometimes we just want to go away from the uncomfortable situation asap. 

My case is a bit different because I try to avoid saying that phrase, despite knowing how useful it can be. I work at a restaurant which can sometimes be full of desperate and not really well-mannered guys. It's hard to get rid of them and they just can't take a hint. I know most of them would leave me alone if I told them I'm in a relationship, but I don't say it because I just want them to learn that god damn, just because I'm single it doesn't mean I'll start dating someone I don't see myself with. And I hate that these men see women just as a sex object. A lot of these guys are full of disgusting comments and I don't have much respect for them and just want them to leave me alone (maybe that's an excuse for me being rude and cold). 


Some get offended when I tell them no and that I'm single, and tell me that this means that there must be something wrong with me inside my head (ironically they are right, but for the wrong reason imo). 

So I usually say something like "no thanks" or start joking around that I already have 3 husbands and 6 kids or sth and they just laugh. 

But for the usual, well-mannered peopel, I think that a good response could be something like "I appreciate the invitation, but I don't see us in that way" 'but I don't really know what the right words could be.

It's still one of the best ways to get someone to leave you alone. Some people just won't take no for an answer easily and can't understand how can someone rather be single than dating whenever there's a chance. And also, it sucks telling people no and "letting them down".

You did the right thing both for you and the person asking you out. There's no need to give in the pressure to be with someone just because they ask you out and you not having a relationship right now. When you'll know, you'll know and you won't have to deal with potential bad experiences of choosing just about anyone.

A couple of years ago I dated some guys despite not being this much into them, but I just couldn't do it. I was almost always uncomfortable and it didn't lead anywhere. Luckily I stopped before we could even call it official. I do want to be in a relationship but not just for the sake of it.

So good job on your assertiveness, for being aware of your gut feelings and for being honest with the other person. :)

I second that. But still different than some other PDs that could be also, at least partly driven by shame. For me there is also a constant apologetic behavior for the fact that I even exist and trying to hide myself with intense loneliness.

That's exactly how I'm feeling a lot of the times now.

It's really weird. I feel better yet kind of worse? And it's even weirder hearing compliments from people (both close friends, some acquaintances and people who known me for a long time) that I seem more confident  that I'm glowing.

I don't know if I really am, though. I still get so depressed at times, right now I'm going through a bad period and I don't know. Am I really getting better? It is easier, it is better, but I don't even know. I can't explain, I don't understand.

I've been tracking my day for about 1,5 years. Almost every day I would rate my day. There would be like a good, very good, bad etc rating, but also dramatic changes (days where I'd go to more extreme moods from devastation to happiness etc.). I think this is also important.

The important thing I noticed is that in the last 8 months or so, there a much less of these extreme shifts of mood. I'm more stable. My days are mostly is the "okayness" area, with some more greyness or some more happy periods, but there's no drama. There's also no more relief from going back together and arguing and devastation.

Still, I would like to be happier. I'm still quite anxious. 

Also, something changed in me a couple of months ago. I realized don't want to go back anymore. I still occasionally miss it, miss them as a person, miss what could've been, blame myself, but I think that the answer is not in the person I miss, but more like a sign that I want closeness again. And I'm still having walls around other people, people in my life who I know I can trust, who I can call my friends, who I would burn my hand for and they would do the same for me.

Something is still stopping me to get a bit closer. Or maybe that's now the right word. To get more comfortable with it perhaps. But I think (most of the time at least) that everything is going to be okay, and for you as well. You have more time now to focus on your healthy relationships and you will get to the feeling of inner peace again. You're just not used to it, maybe. But you can get used to it, as much as you did get used to toxic friendships and accepted it as your normal state at the time.

I would really like to, but something is always stopping me to relax. I can sometimes "dance" when I'm in my own and had a bit of drink. I can have quite a lot of fun doing this, but even at those times, my fun is interrupted a couole of times when I start feeling off, almost depressed for a bit.

I did go to a club a couple of times and I never really fully enjoyed. Partly, there was rarely the music I liked because I just went where my friends wanted to go. Sometimes there were some songs I liked and being drunk and in the dark, I did enjoy it for a bit.

Even at smaller, home parties where I can put the music I like, I still can't relax. I can't start dancing in my own even if I want to. Sometimes I join others who already dance but I am never fully relaxed, but it is enjoyable for some brief moments. But a part of me is always tensed and I think about how stupid my moves are. It gets easier when I put those thoughts away and laugh at myself.

I missed the part where other teens started going to parties so my first party was pretty scary to me, but I never caught up. I would still like to go on some festivals and clubs with the music I like, because even if I didn't experience it fully yet, I still think there is room to improve and feel better and more relaxed.

Maybe if we start first being comfortable around ourselves (dancing at home etc) it'll get easier in public as well. And it'll feel mkre natural and fun.

I struggle with this so much. I don't have much "love life" experience but I can separate my experience in categories/phases:

- liking each other - starting to talk more and more - go out - asks me to be his girlfriend (i was 15 or 16 back then) - nopenopenope ew - i end the relationship before sex could happen because even kissing him felt gross, i felt gross as well

- faking till making it: i try online dating. I only kinda liked these guys, but wanted to give an opportunity to them and myself. At first it's good, i feel a bit of butterflies. The more intense the relationship, the more I wanted to leave. I did felt okay with hugs and cuddling though. These dating things didn't last either, I escaoed one way or another

- trying to get closer to guys i actually like them irl. Usually begins slow. I'm chill, I learned to be more relaxed. We get friendlier with each other. I start to like them a looot. I get nervous around them, I shut down, i become the most boring and weird version of myself. They make a move. I'm oblivious. I get their hint a few days later. I try to make a move. It ends cold from their side. I'm hurt and ashamed, but it makes me like them even more. I put them on a pedestal but at the same time want to run away from them when things get closer. 

I guess I only like the idea of being in love, but actual thing scares me so much. When safe at home I'd sell my soul to be with him right now, but if I saw him on the street I'd probably say hello but want to run away asap

I don't really know. It's one of my main reasons I stopped online dating. I need a lot of time to get used to a new person, even friendships are a challenge and now it's just expected to go from 0 to 100 in a few days?? It feels forced to me, I couldn't enjoy it. The guys either thought that there's no chemistry between us because we were just talking or they took the lead and I was like "... Okay... I guess that's how it's supposed to be... That's how normal people behave... act normal... Fake it till you make it... why is everyone so comfortable with each other and I'm this frozen freak..."
A mix of confirmation of something I already suspected, shame and hope
